- Single-site, modern spinning asset: the FY2023-24 expansion of 41,472 compact spindles was commissioned two months ahead of schedule without time or cost overruns, and the Company states the enhanced capacity let it exceed estimated turnover
- Quality assurance infrastructure - USTER HVI-1000, AFIS PRO 2, UT-5, UTR-4 and CLASSIMAT-5 testing equipment enabling precise quality monitoring and customised product solutions
- Automation across the process chain from blow room to final packing with real-time monitoring, stated to reduce human intervention and improve consistency
- Diversified export footprint (15 countries named, '35+ countries served') plus a domestic base that the Company was able to grow ~6% in FY2025-26 to offset an export decline
- IT/ERP backbone: end-to-end Business Process Management on the Infor LX ERP platform live since 2019, centralised firewalled network connecting manufacturing machines and user computers, McAfee endpoint security, HRMS/payroll, a customised Cotton Bale Management system and an in-house open-source email server for daily departmental reporting
- Captive renewable power: 5.2 MW rooftop solar installed across all units, stated to significantly reduce energy cost
- Repeat business - the Company states its commitment to quality, consistency and timely delivery is reflected in a high level of repeat business
- Workforce of around 800+ people including technical, non-technical, managerial, casual and contract labour, with industrial relations stated as cordial

bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Raw cotton price and availability - single agricultural input, monsoon-dependent — Cotton is the primary raw material for yarn and is an agricultural produce whose supply and quality are subject to forces of nature i.e. monsoon. The Company states any increase in raw cotton prices makes things difficult for the industry, resulting in weak demand and thin margins, and that availability of raw cotton at reasonable prices is crucial for the spinning industry. Compounding this, untimely rainfall in Maharashtra, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana has damaged crops and farmers are shifting to more profitable crops, reducing cultivated area.
- Rising dependence on imported cotton — 'High Import Dependency: Due to low local output, reliance on imported cotton is rising (up 85% YoY in 5M FY2026), increasing costs for manufacturers.' The mitigation cited - a temporary exemption on cotton import duties - was valid only until December 2025, so the cost cushion is stated as expiring.
- US tariff shock and reduced export incentives compressing export profitability — The US imposed a 50% effective tariff on Indian apparel exports in August 2025, trickling down to demand for Indian cotton yarn, with Indian exporters discounting to hold market share and narrowing spinner margins. Separately, RoDTEP export rebates were cut from 3.4% to 1.7% of FOB value, directly impacting export profitability. Lagnam's own export revenue fell ~7.5% in FY2025-26 and export volumes fell to 9,868 MT from 10,335 MT, with margin pressure in H1 attributed to subdued demand in key European markets impacted by US tariff developments.
- Industry margin contraction and falling yarn contribution — Spinners' margins are expected to contract by 50-100 basis points in FY2026, particularly in the second half. Average cotton yarn contributions dropped from Rs. 103/kg in H1 FY2026 to Rs. 96/kg in November 2025.
- Capital intensity plus high interest rates — The Company states the high rate of interest is affecting the financial performance of the textile industry, and that spinning, being more capital intensive, requires huge long-term and short-term working-capital funds; it calls on Government to provide cheap finance so the industry remains financially viable. Structurally relevant to Lagnam, whose borrowings are backed by personal guarantees of the director and a corporate guarantee of a related company.
- Single-product, single-site concentration — Structural concentration disclosed indirectly rather than labelled as a risk: 'As the Company is manufacturing only the one product i.e. Cotton Yarn, Therefore, segment/product-wise details are not applicable', and the whole manufacturing base is one facility at Hamirgarh, Bhilwara, Rajasthan. There is no product, process or geographic diversification to absorb a cotton-cycle or site-level shock.
- Competitive displacement by lower-cost countries and by synthetic fibre — Indian textiles face stiff competition from Bangladesh, Taiwan and other emerging economies and from countries with lower tariff rates; the MD&A also concedes India's runner-up position faces 'stiff chances of being taken away by smaller countries like Vietnam and Bangladesh'. Separately, increasing availability of cheaper synthetic alternatives (polyester/nylon) continues to threaten demand for cotton-based products, and one stated Indian demand driver is an explicit 'shift from cotton to man-made fiber'.
- Geopolitical disruption in export corridors and Chinese demand volatility — Geopolitical instability in neighbouring markets like Bangladesh has disrupted trade, challenging growth in export volumes; and although a recovery in exports to China is expected early in the year, fluctuations in Chinese demand remain a constant risk factor. Currency movement is separately flagged - exchange rate fluctuations affect export pricing and profitability for Indian yarn exporters.
- Compliance and certification cost escalation (QCOs, traceability) — Enforcement of trade regulations such as the Cotton Bales (Quality Control) Order can create barriers for Indian cotton in the global market; the Government is bringing more than 100 QCOs covering the entire textile value chain and the initial investment in labs and connected mandates is stated to be beyond the capacity of the MSME sector that accounts for over 85% of the value chain. The cost of certification to prove sustainability, traceability and circularity is already high and still escalating.
- Governance structure of risk oversight - no dedicated Risk Management Committee — 'The Company has not made Risk Management Committee, but the Board of Directors and Audit Committee is looking after the Risk Management of the Company.' A risk-mapping, exposure, impact and mitigation mechanism is stated to be in place with Heads of Departments responsible for implementation and reporting to the Board and Audit Committee.

outlook.body:
- Consolidate the existing product portfolio and manufacturing capacities rather than add new capacity (Chairman, 'The Road Ahead')
- Expand presence in new domestic and international markets
- Increase the share of value-added yarns in the mix
- Deepen customer relationships across geographies
- Continue investing in advanced technologies, digitalization, research & development, process innovation and continuous upskilling of the workforce
- Deliberately rebalance the sales mix toward the domestic market to mitigate risk from global trade volatility (US tariffs, Iran-Israel conflict), accepting a lower export share to hold total revenue stable
- Continuously expand the portfolio of value-added yarns to address emerging customer needs (stakeholder-value 'CUSTOMERS' section)
- Allocate capital prudently to strengthen competitive position and support long-term value creation (stakeholder-value 'SHAREHOLDERS' section)
- BACK-FILLED FROM SIBLING BUNDLE (risks_esg.txt, MD&A section headed 'STRATEGIES:'): focus on innovation & technology; explore existing potential and new product development; build value around the commodity; product development for immediate market needs; lean manufacturing to minimise waste; asset reliability through smart machinery and AI; organisational alignment with clear assignment of duties; energy - sustainable manufacturing and use of energy-efficient machinery. The MD&A extract routed into THIS bundle skips that block, so it is recorded here with explicit provenance rather than left absent.
- Build a strong talent pipeline through hiring, development and retention, with internal capability building via job rotation and job enrichment (Board's Report item 33)
- Stated philosophy is retention and prudent allocation rather than distribution. The Board's Report (routed into the SIBLING capex_expansion bundle - provenance noted because the governance bundle does not carry the dividend paragraph) states the Company 'remains committed to maximizing long-term shareholder value through disciplined capital allocation' and that the Board 'has chosen to retain profits to fund future growth opportunities and strengthen the financial position of the Company', with no dividend recommended for FY2025-26 and no amount transferred to general reserves. Expansion spending is likewise on hold: no new expansion projects were undertaken during the year, with an emphasis on conserving resources for future growth. The stakeholder-value spread adds that the Company 'allocates capital prudently to strengthen our competitive position' and remains 'committed to sustainable profitability, financial resilience'. Balance-sheet posture disclosures without figures: the Company neither invited nor accepted public deposits; it granted no loans, guarantees or securities and made no investments under Section 186; borrowings are supported by personal guarantees of the director and a corporate guarantee of Lagnam Infotech Solutions Private Limited; there was no one-time settlement with any financial institution and no proceeding pending under the IBC 2016. Related-party transactions were all on arm's-length basis in the ordinary course, so no AOC-2 disclosure was required, and all were placed before the Audit Committee.
- Captive renewable power in place: 5.2 MW of rooftop solar installed across all units, stated to significantly reduce energy costs and enhance sustainability, with rooftop space optimised for maximum renewable utilisation (BACK-FILLED FROM SIBLING BUNDLE capex_expansion.txt, Board's Report item 4 - the risks_esg bundle carries no ESG chapter at all).
- Renewable build-out under way: a 12 MW (DC) solar power plant and a 3.2 MW (AC) hybrid wind-solar power plant 'in process' in Jaisalmer district, Rajasthan, expected to deliver significant power-cost savings on commissioning; no date is attached (BACK-FILLED FROM SIBLING BUNDLE capex_expansion.txt).
- Stated strategy pillar 'Energy - sustainable manufacturing and use of energy efficient machinery' (MD&A 'STRATEGIES:' list, present in this bundle).
- Product-level sustainability claim, unquantified and uncertified in the text: the Company calls its output 'Sustainable Yarn' because it is 'manufactured keeping environment, humans and the economy in balance', asserts its yarns 'do not deplete the earth's resources or cause carbon footprints' and that they are 'organically grown or manufactured by recycling'. No supporting metric, certification or verification is disclosed anywhere in the routed text - flagged as a claim, not an achievement.
- CSR programmes run during FY2025-26 (spend amounts deliberately excluded as financial-note content): Project 'Shiksha', a Social Health Care Project, 'Step against hunger & poverty', Rural Development, Education Empowerment for specially-abled children, Animals Welfare, and a Safe Drinking (water) project - the CSR note truncates mid-item at '(g) Safe Drinking'. Provenance: governance_entities.txt bundle.
- Social/governance controls stated: zero-tolerance POSH policy with NO complaints received during the year (a stated nil, not silence); Whistle Blower / Vigil Mechanism policy under Section 177(9) and Regulation 22; no instances of fraud reported by auditors under Section 143(12); cordial industrial relations with a workforce of around 800+ people; recognition of Rs. 14.99 lakhs incremental past service cost from the New Labour Codes notified 21 November 2025.
- NO BRSR / Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report content was routed into this bundle. There are no emissions, energy-consumption, water, waste, safety or diversity metrics and no dated ESG target anywhere in the six bundles. Every item above is narrative or backfilled - the honest position is that this AR extract discloses no quantified, time-bound ESG target.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: FY2025-26 was a no-new-capex year by explicit choice: 'The Company remains focused on prudent capital allocation and has not undertaken any new expansion projects during the year, with an emphasis on conserving resources for future growth opportunities.' The last spinning expansion was the FY2023-24 project of 41,472 spindles of 100% compact cotton yarn at a total investment of Rs. 218.00 crore, commissioned on 31 January 2024 - two months ahead of the scheduled timeline and, per the MD&A, without any time or cost overruns. That expansion incorporates advanced automation and digitalization, which the Company expects to enhance product quality, improve operational efficiencies and optimize cost structures. The only live projects are in captive power: an existing 5.2 MW rooftop solar capacity installed across all units (milestone journey dates the rooftop solar project to 2025), plus a 12 MW (DC) solar power plant and a 3.2 MW (AC) hybrid wind-solar power plant 'in process' in the District of Jaisalmer, Rajasthan, on commissioning of which the Company expects significant savings in power cost. No commissioning date, cost or funding source is stated for either Jaisalmer project. The Board recommended no dividend for FY2025-26, retaining profits to fund future growth and strengthen the financial position, and transferred no amount to general reserves. Capital commitments contracted but not provided for stood at Rs. 4,324.25 Lacs as at 31 March 2026 against Rs. Nil as at 31 March 2025 - a stated re-appearance of contracted capital spend after a nil prior year, which is the only rupee forward-capex signal in the report.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- During FY 2025-26 the Indian cotton yarn industry witnessed a gradual recovery driven by improved domestic demand and revival in exports, particularly to key markets such as China and Bangladesh
- The industry is expected to record revenue growth in the upcoming years, supported by higher volumes and marginal improvement in yarn realizations
- Domestic consumption continues to account for a major share of yarn demand, while exports contribute nearly 30% of the industry's revenue
- The industry remained exposed to volatility in raw material prices, geopolitical disruptions and changing trade dynamics
- Indian textile and apparel industry projected to grow at a 6.0-7.0% CAGR between fiscal 2024 and fiscal 2028 to Rs. 12,400-12,500 billion in fiscal 2028, with exports growing 4.5-5.5% CAGR and the domestic industry 7.0-8.0% CAGR
- Global textile industry expected to grow at a 2.5-3.5% CAGR between FY2023 and FY2027 to ~USD 1,780-1,830 billion in FY2027; volumes from 193 billion tons in FY2023 to 210-220 billion tons in FY2027 (2.0-3.0% CAGR)
- Cotton expected to remain the largest contributor to the textile industry at ~38-40% share in FY2027, versus around 39% of total textile sales over FY2018-FY2023
- Company-level demand mix driver: the Company states it intentionally moved contribution from export to domestic to maintain stability in business and revenue, with the domestic increase offsetting the export decline
- Company-level margin driver: value-added mix, specifically the addition of 'Compact Cotton Yarn' to the portfolio, together with optimal capacity utilization, cited as the lever behind operating-margin improvement (the Company quantifies this in the Directors' Report; the figures are financial-statement/ratio content and are deliberately NOT reproduced here)
- Export headwind driver: pressure on export margins in the first half of the year due to subdued demand in key European markets impacted by US tariff-related developments; despite this the Company states it remains structurally well-positioned in international markets
- Industry demand tailwinds cited: increase in discretionary income, rising urban population, growth of online retailing, robust growth of technical textiles, and global industry expanding outside of China aiding Indian export markets
- Government/raw-material driver: Union Budget 2025-26 allocated INR 5,272 crore to the Ministry of Textiles (a 19% increase); a multi-year Cotton Productivity Mission and Kasturi Cotton traceability aim to lift yields and positioning of Indian cotton

risks.note: The Company states the high rate of interest is affecting the financial performance of the textile industry, and that spinning, being more capital intensive, requires huge long-term and short-term working-capital funds; it calls on Government to provide cheap finance so the industry remains financially viable. Structurally relevant to Lagnam, whose borrowings are backed by personal guarantees of the director and a corporate guarantee of a related company.
risks.risk: Capital intensity plus high interest rates

risks.note: Structural concentration disclosed indirectly rather than labelled as a risk: 'As the Company is manufacturing only the one product i.e. Cotton Yarn, Therefore, segment/product-wise details are not applicable', and the whole manufacturing base is one facility at Hamirgarh, Bhilwara, Rajasthan. There is no product, process or geographic diversification to absorb a cotton-cycle or site-level shock.

Indian textiles face stiff competition from Bangladesh, Taiwan and other emerging economies and from countries with lower tariff rates; the MD&A also concedes India's runner-up position faces 'stiff chances of being taken away by smaller countries like Vietnam and Bangladesh'. Separately, increasing availability of cheaper synthetic alternatives (polyester/nylon) continues to threaten demand for cotton-based products, and one stated Indian demand driver is an explicit 'shift from cotton to man-made fiber'.
risks.risk: Competitive displacement by lower-cost countries and by synthetic fibre

risks.note: Geopolitical instability in neighbouring markets like Bangladesh has disrupted trade, challenging growth in export volumes; and although a recovery in exports to China is expected early in the year, fluctuations in Chinese demand remain a constant risk factor. Currency movement is separately flagged - exchange rate fluctuations affect export pricing and profitability for Indian yarn exporters.
risks.risk: Geopolitical disruption in export corridors and Chinese demand volatility
